what: Polyn, Natu, Cohen and Kahana (Univ. of Pennsylvania) used fMRI pattern classifiers to show that the category (faces, locations, objects) of items a person was about to recall could be read from brain activity before the verbal recall.
fit: A machine-learning decoder reads the content category of a person's memory recall directly from brain activity, although only at coarse category level, not specific thoughts or images.

sources.title: Category-Specific Cortical Activity Precedes Retrieval During Memory Search
sources.quote: The reappearance of a given category's activity pattern correlates with verbal recalls made from that category and precedes the recall event by several seconds.

note: Replaces the second pass (ATR/Kyoto 2008 10x10-pixel reconstruction of SEEN images), which is decoding of perception, not of thoughts or memories. Polyn 2005 is the earliest fitting item found: it decodes recalled (remembered) content, though only the category. Considered and rejected: Kamitani and Tong 2005 (decodes seen oriented gratings, perception); Haxby 2001 (seen object categories); Yang Dan 1999 (cat thalamus, animal and seen images); P300 'guilty knowledge' / brain-fingerprinting tests of 1988-91 (EEG detects recognition of a given probe item, not reading unknown content, so a lie-detector rather than a thought reader); Haynes 2007 intention decoding and Horikawa 2013 dream decoding (later); 2025 'mind captioning' of recalled content (later). Borderline fit, hence low.
searched: Crossref record for Polyn et al. 2005 (quote verified with the helper); Wikipedia brain-computer-interface page; the other candidates (Kamitani and Tong 2005, Haxby 2001, Dan 1999, P300 concealed-information tests, Haynes 2007) were judged from background knowledge, not fetched. No separate web search was run. Search hint (imagined content, memories, specific thoughts): no pre-2005 decoding of memories or thoughts found.

concept_note: Second pass (2008 ATR reconstruction of seen 10x10 images) rejected as perception decoding, not thoughts or memories; replaced by Polyn et al. 2005 fMRI decoding of the category of recalled items, a coarse but real memory-content decoder (low confidence, borderline). No first_practical_use or mass_adoption: no use of thought or memory decoding outside the lab.

what: Volvo's Kalmar car plant (Sweden, opened 1974) moved car bodies and engines on a fleet of about 250 battery-powered, computer-guided assembly carriers.
fit: A computer guides a whole fleet of driverless self-moving carriers; the source says only 'computer-guided', so the central-computer coordination is inferred, not quoted.

sources.title: Architecture Plus, November 12, 1974
sources.quote: battery-powered and computer-guided, that creep silently about the factory bearing body assemblies

note: Replaces Kiva 2006/2007 in the second pass, which is too late. Volvo Kalmar (1974) is the earliest dated computer-guided driverless fleet found. Caveat: the fetchable page does not say a single central computer directs the carriers; sources that do say so (Management planning and control systems 1977; Time 1974-11-11; People at Work 1977) are lending-library or did not yield the text, so unverified. Rejected: 1950s Barrett driverless tractors (wire-guided, not computer directed); Tetra Pak Lund 1976 (no fetchable source); Kiva/Walgreens 2007 and Staples 2006 (later).
searched: ia_search3 for 'central computer' 'guided vehicles' 1970-1982, 'driverless tractors computer control' 1960-1975, 'computer-controlled automatic guided vehicle' 1975-1983, 'driverless central computer vehicles dispatch' 1965-1984, Computerworld AGV 1978-86, Kalmar carriers computer 1973-78; Wikipedia AGV, Kalmar, Kiva pages. Computer-integrated-manufacturing (1974) hit about dispatching operatorless trucks from a central computer is a lending book (401), not readable.

what: Volvo Kalmar assembly plant in regular production use of its fleet of computer-guided carriers.
fit: Same event: the carriers did the plant's real production work under computer guidance, but the central-coordination detail is not quoted from a fetched page.

sources.title: Architecture Plus, November 12, 1974
sources.quote: forms of "carriers," battery-powered and computer-guided, that creep silently about the factory bearing body assemblies

note: Same event as the demonstration, so same date. Replaces Walgreens/Kiva 2007. Fit is partial (computer-guided fleet; central control inferred).

concept_note: Moved earlier from 2007 (Kiva/Walgreens) to 1974 (Volvo Kalmar computer-guided carriers); fit is partial because the fetched page does not name a central computer, so confidence is low. No mass_adoption milestone: fleet management of warehouse robots became routine only in the 2010s and no source was fetched.

what: RCA Laboratories (Harry Olson and Herbert Belar, Princeton) built a phonetic typewriter model that typed spoken sounds; reported in J. Acoust. Soc. Am. in 1956 and confirmed by RCA to the press in August 1956.
fit: A machine listens to speech and types the words automatically, as a single-talker laboratory model with a small vocabulary.

sources.publisher: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America (Crossref record)
sources.title: Phonetic Typewriter
sources.quote: a simplified model of a phonetic typewriter has been developed incorporating all of these aspects

sources.title: The Atlanta Constitution, 2 August 1956
sources.quote: is a phonetic typewriter using an electronic brain to memorize words

sources.title: Challenge August-September 1956
sources.quote: developed a model of such a voice-operated typewriter which is 80 per cent accurate

note: Replaces the second pass (Kyoto Sonotype 1961). Earlier candidates: Steno-Sonograph (Electronics, Sept 1950; fetched) prints visual sound characters for a human stenographer to read and 'is not yet perfected', so no text output, rejected; Typo-Sonograph in the same article was only under construction; Bell Labs 1952 digit recognizer (Audrey) recognizes ten spoken digits, not dictation text. Date 1956-07 is the JASA record date (the abstract appeared in the 1956 volume; full paper Nov 1956); Kyoto 1960-61 and Tangora 1980s are later.
searched: ia_search3 for 'phonetic typewriter' 1950-1958 (found JASA 1956, Challenge 1956, Acoustical Engineering 1957, Wisdom 1956, Atlanta Constitution); page_text3 on Electronics 1950-09 (Steno-Sonograph); Crossref JASA records. Pre-1950 typing-from-speech machines not searched separately.

what: Kurzweil Applied Intelligence officially released its 1,000-word Voicerad system in Boston in December 1986; a radiologist was already writing his reports with it by voice. Dragon Systems had announced Voicescribe-1000 'automatic dictation transcription system' in June 1986.
fit: A computer listens to a user's spoken dictation of reports and produces the edited, printed text, used by a working radiologist.

sources.title: Voice system cures MD ills
sources.quote: allows radiologists to dictate, edit and print out diagnostic X-ray reports by voice

sources.title: Speech transcriber announced
sources.quote: announced Voicescribe-1000, an automatic dictation transcription system

note: Replaces Dragon Dictate 1990 in the second pass: Kurzweil Voicerad and Dragon Voicescribe-1000 were dictation products in 1986 (PC Magazine 27 Oct 1987 also lists both). Earlier: Threshold Technology voice input from 1972 was data entry of commands, not dictation; Kurzweil 1985 Voice Report not found in searches. Voicescribe-1000 was only announced in June 1986 (availability not shown), so Voicerad December 1986 is the first documented in use. Limited vocabulary and discrete speech, so a strict dictation fit but narrow.
searched: Computerworld 1986 via ia_search3 and page_text3; ia_search3 for 'Kurzweil' 'Voice Report' 1985-87 and Kurzweil radiolog in Computerworld 1985-86 (0 hits); PC Magazine 1987-10-27 quote checked FOUND.

concept_note: First demonstration moved from Kyoto 1961 to RCA phonetic typewriter 1956 (now sourced contemporaneously); first practical use moved from Dragon Dictate 1990 to Kurzweil Voicerad Dec 1986 (Dragon Voicescribe announced June 1986). No mass_adoption: routine speech dictation on smartphones/PCs came later and no fetched source dates it.
